content: Short stature is defined as a height that is more than two standard deviations below the mean for a given chronological age and sex. This corresponds to a linear height below the 3rd percentile. The most common causes of short stature are normal variations in growth, such as familial short stature and constitutional delay of growth and puberty. There is no established system for classifying short stature. However, based on etiology, it can be categorized into normal variants of growth or systemic pathological causes. Normal variants include familial short stature, constitutional delay of growth and puberty, small for gestational age with catch-up growth, and idiopathic short stature. Pathological causes include malnutrition, glucocorticoid treatment, endocrine disorders (e.g., growth hormone deficiency, hypothyroidism, Cushing's syndrome, rickets, type 1 diabetes mellitus), genetic syndromes (e.g., Turner syndrome, Noonan syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, Russell-Silver syndrome, achondroplasia), systemic diseases (e.g., celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, cystic fibrosis, congenital heart disease, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, juvenile arthritis, sickle cell anemia, immunodeficiencies, parasitic infections), and environmental factors like lead exposure. The pathophysiology of short stature involves multiple factors affecting the growth plate cartilage of bones. These include genetic factors (e.g., GH gene mutations, SHOX gene variants, Turner syndrome, achondroplasia), growth-promoting hormones (e.g., growth hormone, thyroid hormone, IGF-1, testosterone), growth-inhibiting hormones (e.g., glucocorticoids, estrogen), paracrine factors (e.g., fibroblast growth factor, parathyroid hormone-related protein), and extracellular matrix proteins (e.g., collagen, proteoglycans). The prevalence of short stature varies depending on environmental and genetic factors. Growth hormone deficiency, for example, has a prevalence of approximately 1 in 1,348 in the United States, with males being more commonly affected. There is no racial predilection for short stature. Risk factors for short stature include genetic predisposition, environmental influences, poor maternal or infant nutrition, low birth weight, and low gestational age at birth. Screening for short stature involves serial measurements of linear height and height velocity, charted at every well-child visit. The infancy-childhood-puberty model can help detect abnormalities. During infancy, growth is nutrition-dependent, with rapid linear growth of 30-35 cm. In childhood, growth is growth hormone-dependent, with a constant height velocity. During puberty, sex steroids and growth hormone drive the pubertal growth spurt, typically occurring around age 10 in girls and age 12 in boys. If untreated, short stature results in a lower-than-normal adult height. Diagnosis is based on the definition of height more than two standard deviations below the mean for age and sex. Serial height measurements and growth charts are essential. For infants under two years, length is measured lying down, while standing height is measured for children over two years. The history and symptoms of short stature often include a history of premature birth, small for gestational age, malnutrition, weight loss, or symptoms of underlying conditions like Crohn's disease, hypothyroidism, Cushing's syndrome, or recurrent infections. Physical examination should include plotting height and weight on growth charts, assessing height velocity, calculating midparental height, and evaluating bone age. Bone age may be delayed (e.g., constitutional delay, systemic illness), normal (e.g., familial short stature), or advanced (e.g., precocious puberty). Laboratory findings are not specific to short stature but may reveal abnormalities related to underlying conditions. For example, growth hormone deficiency may show low growth hormone levels and low IGF-1. Hypothyroidism may present with low thyroid hormone and high TSH. Karyotyping may be useful for genetic syndromes, and IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies may indicate celiac disease. Imaging studies, such as X-rays, can determine bone age. MRI may be helpful in cases of growth hormone deficiency, showing findings like an absent anterior pituitary gland, ectopic posterior pituitary gland, or pituitary hypoplasia. Echocardiography or ultrasound may assist in diagnosing congenital heart disease. CT scans and other imaging modalities are generally not associated with short stature. The primary treatment for short stature due to growth hormone deficiency is growth hormone replacement therapy using recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH). The initial dose is weight-based, typically starting at 25 μg/kg/day and adjusted based on growth response and IGF-1 levels. Other pharmacologic therapies may include recombinant IGF-1, testosterone, aromatase inhibitors (e.g., anastrozole, letrozole), estrogen, or GnRH analogs, depending on the underlying cause. Patients with specific disorders causing short stature should receive targeted treatment for those conditions. Surgical intervention is not recommended for managing short stature. There are no established measures for primary or secondary prevention of short stature, but adequate maternal nutrition during pregnancy is an important factor.
